📁 projects/tsp_visualiser.py
Project case study

Travelling Salesman Visualiser

An interactive Streamlit app that solves the Travelling Salesman Problem for real-world locations, comparing an exact algorithm against a fast heuristic, live, on a satellite map.

Streamlit geopy PyDeck Algorithms Matplotlib
Watch the Demo View GitHub
01
Project overview

An interactive Streamlit app that solves the Travelling Salesman Problem for a set of real-world locations: place names are geocoded live with geopy, both algorithms solve the route, and PyDeck renders it on a live satellite map.

The two demos below run on the exact same 6 UK cities (Cheltenham, Manchester, London, Birmingham, Leeds and Oxford), so you can compare how each algorithm actually thinks, not just how fast it runs. Built as my A-Level Computer Science NEA project.

02
Key findings
649.22 km
Brute Force — optimal route
Checks every possible ordering of the 6 cities and guarantees the shortest route.
684.61 km
Nearest Neighbour — greedy route
Runs far faster, but isn't guaranteed to find the optimal path.
~5.5%
Longer than optimal
The gap between the fast heuristic and the guaranteed-best answer, on this 6-city route.
03
Watch it work
Brute Force649.22 km
Nearest Neighbour684.61 km

Same route, same 6 cities: Brute Force (left) checks every possible ordering before picking the shortest, while Nearest Neighbour (right) greedily jumps to whichever unvisited city is closest at each step.

04
How the algorithms differ

Both algorithms solve the same problem. The difference is the trade-off between a guaranteed answer and speed.

01
Brute Force checks every possible ordering of the cities (5! = 120 routes once the start city is fixed) and picks the shortest.
Guarantees the optimal answer, but the number of routes to check grows factorially, so it only stays fast for a small number of locations.
02
Nearest Neighbour is a greedy heuristic: starting from one city, it always jumps to whichever unvisited city is closest, and repeats until every city has been visited.
Far faster and scales to many more locations, but isn't guaranteed to find the shortest route. Here it comes in about 5.5% longer than the Brute Force optimum.
05
Tools & techniques
Geocoding
geopy live place-name lookup
Routing algorithms
Brute Force (permutations) Nearest Neighbour (greedy)
Visualisation
PyDeck live map rendering Matplotlib
Interface
Streamlit interactive web app

This was my first real dive into algorithms and interactive visualisation: building both an exact solver and a fast heuristic, then giving them an actual map to run on rather than just printing a distance in a terminal.

📁 projects/retail_sql.sql
Project case study

Retail Sales Performance Analysis

Turning 1,000 supermarket transactions into actionable business insights using MySQL.

MySQL SQL Data Cleaning Business Analysis Window Functions
View SQL Analysis View GitHub
01
Project overview

The dataset covers 1,000 individual supermarket transactions across 3 branches and 6 product lines, recorded between January and March 2019. The business problem: which products, branches, times and customer segments actually drive revenue, and where the opportunities for improvement are.

Using MySQL, I investigated revenue by product line and branch, time-of-day and monthly sales patterns, Member vs Normal customer behaviour, and product ratings, then worked to turn each result into a plain-English business finding rather than stopping at the raw numbers.

02

The highest-revenue product line in the dataset.

Highest of all 3 branches, and the highest gross income, despite having the fewest transactions.

Members spend about 3% more per transaction on average.

The highest customer satisfaction score of any product line.
03
What the analysis means

These are analytical recommendations based on patterns in the data, not proven causal relationships.

01
Branch C has a meaningfully higher average transaction value (£337.10) than A and B, despite fewer transactions.
Worth investigating Branch C's product mix, customer behaviour and upselling practices, rather than simply trying to increase footfall.
02
Each branch peaks at a different hour of day (A 11am, B 4pm, C 7pm).
Staffing tailored per branch would likely serve customers better than one company-wide schedule.
03
Each branch has a different top-performing product category.
Inventory and promotions could be adapted to local demand rather than applied uniformly across branches.
04
Members spend slightly more on average and generate more total revenue.
Supports continued investment in the loyalty programme, though this alone doesn't prove the programme causes the higher spend.
04
SQL techniques
Data cleaning
STR_TO_DATE() ALTER TABLE DATE / TIME conversion
Aggregation
SUM() AVG() COUNT() GROUP BY ORDER BY
Time analysis
MONTH() HOUR() DAYNAME()
Advanced SQL
CTEs RANK() OVER() PARTITION BY CASE
05
Featured SQL
A · date cleaning
-- convert the imported text date into a proper DATE column ALTER TABLE sales ADD COLUMN sale_date DATE; UPDATE sales SET sale_date = STR_TO_DATE(Date, '%m/%d/%Y');

Demonstrates cleaning an imported text date into a real MySQL DATE type so it can be used in time-based analysis.

B · branch performance
SELECT branch, COUNT(*) AS transactions, SUM(Total) AS revenue, AVG(Total) AS avg_transaction_value FROM sales GROUP BY branch ORDER BY revenue DESC;

Demonstrates aggregating transactions per branch to compare revenue, volume and average spend side by side.

C · branch-level product ranking
WITH ranked AS ( SELECT branch, `Product line`, SUM(Total) AS revenue, RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY branch ORDER BY SUM(Total) DESC) AS rank_in_branch FROM sales GROUP BY branch, `Product line` ) SELECT branch, `Product line`, revenue FROM ranked WHERE rank_in_branch = 1;

Demonstrates a window function ranking product lines within each branch, restarting the ranking per branch instead of once across the whole table.

06
Going beyond the obvious

The overall company-wide peak was 7pm, but branch-level analysis revealed that this wasn't a universal pattern.

BRANCH A
11am
BRANCH B
4pm
BRANCH C
7pm

Averaged across the whole company, 7pm looks like the answer to "when do we get busiest?", but that number only happens to match Branch C. Segmenting by branch shows three genuinely different patterns, which is a more useful (and more actionable) insight than the single company-wide average. The same applies to top-performing product lines: each branch leads with a different category, a pattern invisible from the overall totals alone.

📁 projects/crime_analysis.ipynb
Project case study

Gloucestershire Crime Analysis

Two years of Gloucestershire Constabulary crime data, cleaned and analysed to find out whether crime is actually changing, or just feels that way.

pandas Matplotlib Seaborn Jupyter EDA Data Cleaning
View Full Analysis View GitHub
01
Project overview

117,553 street-crime records, 24 monthly files, one question I kept coming back to: is crime in Gloucestershire actually changing, or does it just feel that way month to month?

I cleaned and combined two years of Gloucestershire Constabulary data (Jan 2024 – Dec 2025) into a single dataset and worked through 8 questions: what's most common, whether it's rising or falling, where it's concentrated, and what actually happens to a case once it's reported, using pandas, Matplotlib and Seaborn.

02
Key findings
43,236
Violence and sexual offences
The most commonly recorded crime type, about 37% of everything logged.
58,948vs58,605
Records, 2024 vs 2025
−0.58% year-on-year, essentially flat overall.
+928
Anti-social behaviour, YoY change
The single largest increase, bigger than every other rise combined.
−580
Violence & sexual offences, YoY change
The largest decrease, more than offsetting ASB's rise on its own.
GloucestervsCotswold
Highest vs lowest crime district
Raw counts, not population-adjusted. The two city districts alone account for over half of everything recorded.
77.7%
Cases with no suspect ever charged
44.8% unable to prosecute + 32.9% investigation complete, no suspect identified.
03
What the findings mean

These are read from patterns in the data, not causal explanations.

01
Anti-social behaviour rose sharply (+928) while violence and sexual offences fell (−580), roughly offsetting each other.
The flat "−0.58%" headline hides real movement underneath: a single year-on-year number understates how much shifted between categories.
02
44.8% of cases closed as "unable to prosecute suspect" and a further 32.9% as "investigation complete, no suspect identified."
77.7% of recorded cases ended without a charge. The breakdown doesn't show which crime types drove that split, so this describes the outcome, not the reason for it.
03
Gloucester and Cheltenham together account for over half of all recorded crime.
These are raw counts, not rates. The two city districts simply have more people living there, so this reads as a volume story rather than evidence they're more dangerous per person.
04
Around 10,128 Anti-social behaviour records looked like exact duplicates of each other.
ASB reports don't carry a Crime ID or precise timestamp, so there was no reliable way to separate genuine duplicates from separate reports at the same rough time and place, so they were kept rather than guessed away.
04
Data cleaning decisions
[1]
# cleaning decisions, not just cleaning steps dropped = ["Reported by", "Falls within", "Context", "Crime ID"] geography_missing = "3,517 records (~3%), kept, excluded only from location-based questions" outcome_missing = "all belonged to ASB, labelled 'Not applicable (ASB)' rather than dropped"
The first three columns were dropped because they held a single repeated value or were entirely empty, not decisions, just dead weight. Crime ID came out too, but only after checking it was a true unique identifier with no duplicates and confirming every missing ID belonged to Anti-social behaviour. ASB itself doesn't carry a resolvable outcome, so rather than deleting those rows, missing outcomes were labelled explicitly instead of silently dropped. Around 3,517 records (~3%) were missing coordinates entirely, kept in the dataset and only excluded from the questions that specifically needed location.
05
Charts & analysis
58,948
records in 2024
58,605
records in 2025
−0.58%
year-on-year change

Recorded crime was essentially flat between the two years, but flat overall hid real movement underneath: Anti-social behaviour rose by 928 records while the three largest falls (Violence and sexual offences (−580), Public order (−556) and Other theft (−467)) nearly offset it, and May was the busiest month in both years.

Q: did crime volume follow a similar month-to-month pattern in 2024 and 2025, or did one year look meaningfully different?

output: monthly crime count by year

Q: which crime categories were most and least common overall?

output: recorded crime by category

Violence and sexual offences alone accounted for 43,236 records. Together with ASB and shoplifting, the top 3 categories made up roughly 65% of everything recorded.

Q: which crime types grew or shrank the most between 2024 and 2025?

output: change in recorded crime by type, 2024 → 2025

Anti-social behaviour is the clear outlier, up 928 records on its own, more than every other increase combined. Everything below the zero line fell, led by violence and sexual offences, public order and other theft.

Q: which districts had the most recorded crime, and how much of the total did they account for?

output: recorded crimes by district

Gloucester and Cheltenham, the two city districts, together account for over half of all recorded crime. These are raw counts, not rates, so they partly just reflect where more people live.

06
Outcomes & where crime happens
What typically happened to a reported case
44.8% of cases closed as "unable to prosecute suspect" and a further 32.9% closed as "investigation complete, no suspect identified". Together, 77.7% of recorded cases ended with no suspect ever charged. Only a small share progressed to a caution, charge or court outcome. The breakdown here doesn't show which crime types drove that split, so the honest read is that most recorded cases in this dataset didn't end in a charge, not why.

→ show all 11 outcome categories
The district picture is about volume, not a different mix
Violence and sexual offences was the single most recorded crime type in every district, not just city centres. Gloucester and Cheltenham see proportionally more ASB, while rural districts like Cotswold and Forest of Dean see a slightly larger share of vehicle crime and theft, but the overall composition is broadly similar everywhere. The higher raw counts in the cities look like a volume story, not a fundamentally different crime pattern.

08
Limitations

This dataset only captures crime that was reported to and recorded by the police. It says nothing about unreported crime. District counts aren't adjusted for population, so Gloucester and Cheltenham's higher totals partly just reflect more people living there. Around 10,128 Anti-social behaviour records looked like exact duplicates of each other, but ASB reports don't carry a Crime ID or precise timestamp, so there was no reliable way to tell repeated data apart from separate reports at the same rough time and place, so they were kept rather than guessed away. And outcome categories reflect the case status at the time the data was published, not necessarily its final resolution.

This wasn't a clean, ready-to-plot dataset. It came with duplicate-looking records, missing outcomes and columns that needed a real judgment call, not a one-line dropna(). Working through it question by question was as much about knowing what a number can support, and saying so when it can't, as it was about the code itself.
